Call APIs with the Fetch wrapper or generate typed methods from OpenAPI.

The `@restfx/client` package works with the standard Fetch API and does not
require Node.js APIs at runtime.

## Use the Fetch wrapper

Use `createClient()` to configure a base URL, shared headers, and Fetch
credentials:

```ts
import { createClient } from "@restfx/client";

const client = createClient({
  baseUrl: "https://api.example.test/v1/",
  headers: { authorization: `Bearer ${token}` },
  credentials: "include",
});

const response = await client.request("users", { method: "GET" });
if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Request failed: ${response.status}`);
const users: unknown = await response.json();
```

The wrapper returns the standard `Response`; your application handles status
codes and parses the response body. For cross-origin browser requests with
`credentials: "include"`, configure credentialed CORS on the server and ensure
the cookies satisfy browser policies.

## Generate an API client

The generator creates typed operation methods from the server's OpenAPI
document. Build the client package and run the generator from the workspace:

```sh
pnpm --filter @restfx/client build
pnpm --filter @restfx/client generate -- \
  --spec http://localhost:3000/openapi.json \
  --models ./models.js \
  --out ../../apps/playground/src/api-client.ts
```

The `--models` module exports the decorated model classes referenced by the
OpenAPI document. Generated methods validate model-backed requests before
sending them, but the server must still validate every request independently.
Generated clients also expose `ApiError` for non-success HTTP responses.

The generated client supports path, query, and header parameters and JSON,
multipart, URL-encoded, text, and binary bodies. For a request declaring several
media types, it uses the first one in the OpenAPI document. Model validation
errors are thrown before Fetch; non-2xx responses throw `ApiError` with the
status and parsed body, while network failures pass through. Generated response
types are derived from OpenAPI; they do not add runtime response validation.

OpenAPI cookie parameters are not currently supported by the generator. Use
Fetch `credentials` for browser-managed cookies (with appropriate server CORS
and cookie settings); it does not let a browser client set an arbitrary `Cookie`
header. The generator reads RestFX model references from `x-restfx-*` metadata,
so the `--models` module must export those runtime model classes.

See the [`@restfx/client` README](https://github.com/thinkcraft/restfx/blob/main/packages/client/README.md)
for command arguments, supported request and response body types, and runtime
configuration.

Register services and resolve singleton or request-scoped dependencies.

@restfx/server includes a small synchronous IoC container. Register services on a root IocContainer and pass it to HttpServer. Each request gets an isolated scope that shares registrations and singleton instances.

Register and inject services

Section titled “Register and inject services”

Use a class, string, or symbol as a service token. @Inject(token) injects an instance field on resources or services:

The singleton Clock instance is shared across requests. The request-lifetime value is created once per request scope and reused within that request. A service can also resolve dependencies using the container passed to its factory. Services created by the container have their own @Inject fields resolved automatically.

Lifetimes and registration

Section titled “Lifetimes and registration”
  • registerSingleton(token, factoryOrInstance) registers a shared instance. A factory is called on first resolution; use registerInstance(token, value) when the service value itself is a function.
  • registerRequest(token, factory) creates one instance per request scope.
  • register(token, factory, { lifetime: "singleton" | "request" }) selects the lifetime explicitly; request lifetime is the default.
  • get(classToken) automatically constructs an unregistered class with request lifetime. Unregistered string and symbol tokens are errors.

Registration must happen on the root container before requests start. A request scope is available as context.container; resolving a request-lifetime registration directly from the root container throws because there is no active request. IocContainer is synchronous and uses field injection, not constructor injection. Circular factory dependencies throw an error. @Inject supports instance fields, not static or JavaScript #private fields.

The playground demonstrates the pattern in its createPlaygroundContainer factory and passes that container to HttpServer.

Build TypeScript HTTP APIs with shared models, runtime validation, and typed clients.
Share runtime-validated models between your TypeScript server and client.

RestFX is a TypeScript-first framework for building HTTP APIs. Its packages keep
shared models browser-safe while separating Node.js server behavior from Fetch
clients.

## The packages

- **[`@restfx/core`](./models/)** — shared models, field types, runtime
  validation, and typed configuration.
- **[`@restfx/server`](./server/)** — a Node.js HTTP server with decorated
  resources, middleware, request parsing, and OpenAPI generation.
- **[`@restfx/client`](./client/)** — a Fetch wrapper and a generator for typed
  clients from OpenAPI documents.

Apply request middleware to resources and configure cross-origin access.

@HttpMiddleware(handler) attaches middleware to a resource and its nested resources. Middleware runs in order from ancestor to child and can continue the chain, short-circuit it, or wrap the downstream result.

Write middleware

Section titled “Write middleware”

Middleware receives an HttpContext and an async next function. Use context.state to share request-local data with later middleware or the handler:

Middleware can set response headers with context.res.setHeader(). The request’s context.state starts empty for each request; applications can augment the exported HttpContextState interface to type custom properties. Middleware exceptions follow the same server error handling as handler exceptions.

Configure CORS

Section titled “Configure CORS”

Apply @CorsMiddleware(options) to the root resource to handle CORS headers and preflight requests:

origins accepts exact HTTP(S) origins and host patterns. A host-only wildcard matches subdomains at any depth but not the apex domain, and allows either scheme and any port. For example, https://*.preview.example.com restricts the scheme; including a port restricts that too. Matching origins are echoed in Access-Control-Allow-Origin, so credentialed requests work with an explicit allowlist rather than *. Non-matching origins receive no CORS allow headers.

Preflight methods default to methods registered on the resource, including implicit HEAD and OPTIONS; methods can override that list. If allowedHeaders is omitted, requested preflight headers are reflected. The middleware adds relevant Vary headers. CORS is a browser access policy, not an authentication or authorization mechanism.

For cookie-based browser calls, pair credentials: "include" in the client with credentials: true and an explicit allowed origin on the server. Browser cookie SameSite, Secure, and domain rules still apply.
Define shared TypeScript models and validate untrusted input at runtime.

The @restfx/core package provides browser-safe model decorators, field types, and runtime validation. The same model metadata can be used by server routes, OpenAPI generation, and generated clients. Core has no Node.js or HTTP-server dependency, so model classes can be imported by both browser and server code.

Define a model

Section titled “Define a model”

Decorate a class with @Model() and each accepted property with @Field():

Validation does not invoke the model constructor. It returns an instance containing declared fields, with nested models validated recursively. Invalid input throws ModelValidationError; its issues array contains { path, message } entries (for example, address.city). Models strip unknown fields by default; use @Model({ unknownFields: "reject" }) to reject them. The policy can also be overridden for an individual call with validateModel(value, ModelClass, { unknownFields: "reject" }).

Field types and constraints

Section titled “Field types and constraints”

Built-in field types exported by core are:

  • StringField, BooleanField, NumberField, and IntegerField.
  • Email and UUID, which validate strings and emit schema formats.
  • DateField, TimeField, and DateTimeField, which validate ISO/RFC 3339 strings. Values remain strings; they are not converted to JavaScript Dates.
  • Enum([...]) for a fixed set of values.
  • ArrayOf(FieldType | Model) for arrays.
  • UnionOf(...FieldTypes) and DiscriminatedUnion(key, variants) for union values and decorated model variants.

@Field options describe presence, constraints, and schema documentation:

Option Behavior
optional Allows the property to be omitted.
nullable Allows explicit null; omission still depends on optional.
default Used only when omitted. Object defaults are cloned; defaults are checked against the field type and constraints.
minLength, maxLength, pattern Constrain strings. pattern takes a RegExp.
minimum, maximum Constrain numbers.
minItems, maxItems, uniqueItems Constrain array size and uniqueness.
description, examples, deprecated Add documentation metadata to generated schemas.
schema Adds JSON Schema keywords, especially for custom field types.

Constraints are checked at runtime and represented in generated JSON Schema and OpenAPI where supported. Schema metadata does not perform runtime validation; enforce application rules with a field type or model validator too.

Nested models and inheritance

Section titled “Nested models and inheritance”

Use model to compose a decorated model as a nested object. Derived models inherit decorated base fields and model options; a derived field with the same name overrides the inherited field:

Nested values become model instances without calling constructors. Base and derived model validators both run. Schema keywords merge across inheritance, with derived keys taking precedence.

Cross-field validation

Section titled “Cross-field validation”

Use a model-level validate callback when correctness depends on multiple fields. It runs after field validation and may return no issue, one issue, or an array of issues:

Request-source metadata

Section titled “Request-source metadata”

Core fields can declare source: "path" | "query" | "header" and an optional sourceName for the external parameter name. A nested model can use source: "body". This metadata lets one model describe both the shape and validation rules and where the server reads each value. Core itself does not parse HTTP input; see combined request models.

Typed configuration

Section titled “Typed configuration”

defineConfig() preserves and type-checks an object against the small FrameworkConfig shape, which currently contains an optional port:

It does not load files, read environment variables, or start the server; the application chooses how configuration is sourced and applied.

For the full reference, see the @restfx/core README.

Generate an OpenAPI 3.1 document and optional interactive reference UI.

@restfx/server generates an OpenAPI 3.1 document from registered routes, decorator options, and @restfx/core model metadata. Add @OpenApiMiddleware(options) to the root resource:

The endpoint defaults to /openapi.json, serves GET and HEAD, answers OPTIONS, and returns 405 for other methods. The document is generated on the first GET or HEAD and cached. Root middleware runs before the OpenAPI response. The configured path must be an absolute URL path and must not overlap an application route.

Add operation metadata

Section titled “Add operation metadata”

HTTP method decorators accept OpenAPI operation fields such as summary, description, operationId, tags, deprecated, parameters, and security. They also accept requestBody, responses, and the model shortcuts body, request, and response:

Use @HttpResource({ path, tag, description }) to add a resource prefix and describe its OpenAPI tag. Use @Model({ description }) for model descriptions. Operation IDs must be unique. By default, the method name is used when unique; set operationId explicitly when method names are repeated or route variants need stable names. Optional final route parameters generate both path variants.

Routes contribute methods and paths, inferred path parameters, model schemas, and standard request-validation responses. Built-in types and field constraints map to JSON Schema; semantic types like UUID and Email also emit their formats. For non-model response bodies, document the response schema and content type in responses. A custom field’s schema metadata enriches the generated schema but does not perform runtime validation.

Serve a reference UI

Section titled “Serve a reference UI”

Set ui to expose an interactive explorer alongside the JSON document:

Choose type: "scalar", "swagger", or "redoc"; the UI path defaults to /docs and must differ from the document path. The UI HTML loads its UI bundle from a third-party CDN (Scalar from jsDelivr, Swagger UI from unpkg, or Redoc from cdn.redoc.ly). Consider the external network and Content Security Policy implications for your deployment. Omit ui to serve only the JSON document.

OpenAPI generation describes the HTTP contract; it does not replace runtime validation or authentication. Security schemes and operation security describe the contract only; they do not authenticate requests. See model validation and request handling for runtime behavior. The client generator consumes this document; see typed clients.
Configure error handling, observability hooks, proxy trust, and shutdown.

HttpServer wraps Node’s node:http server and accepts framework options as its second constructor argument. It can be used alongside Node HTTP server configuration without moving transport-specific code into @restfx/core.

Errors and observability

Section titled “Errors and observability”

By default, HttpError responses preserve their status and details, while unexpected errors produce a generic 500. Set errorHandler to customize the response. onRequest, onError, and onResponse hooks are useful for logging and metrics; hook failures are isolated so they do not change request behavior:

errorHandler is not called after response headers have been sent. Streaming errors after data has started close the connection because a replacement error response is no longer possible. onResponse reports status, duration, and whether the response completed.

Each request gets a context.requestId. A valid incoming X-Request-Id token (1–128 characters) is retained; otherwise the server creates a UUID. The ID is returned in the response header and is available to hooks. Treat a client supplied ID as a correlation value, never as identity or authorization data.

Node server options and lifecycle

Section titled “Node server options and lifecycle”

Pass serverOptions through to Node’s http.createServer() (for example, headersTimeout and requestTimeout). listen(port = 3000) returns the Node Server instance. await server.close() stops accepting connections and waits for active requests; close({ timeoutMs }) force-closes remaining connections after the timeout. Closing before listening is safe.

Reverse proxies

Section titled “Reverse proxies”

Forwarded headers are ignored unless the connecting peer is trusted. Configure trustProxy as a predicate over the remote socket address, and trust only the addresses of your actual proxy:

For a trusted peer, the server uses validated singular X-Forwarded-Host and X-Forwarded-Proto values (http or https). Configure proxies to overwrite or sanitize forwarded headers. Do not trust arbitrary clients or broad address ranges without an explicit network boundary.

Configuration and examples

Section titled “Configuration and examples”

Core’s defineConfig() is a typed helper for application configuration, not an environment loader. Read environment variables and validate deployment settings in your application, then pass the chosen port and server options to HttpServer. The playground shows this with structured logging and an injected service container.
Validate request sources, parse bounded bodies, use cookies, and stream data.

Each handler receives an HttpContext with req, res, cookies, container, state, and an abort signal. context.req.url is a URL; path excludes the query string, and params contains decoded route parameters.

Routes and parameters

Section titled “Routes and parameters”

@HttpResource(path?) marks a resource class. Resource-valued fields mount nested resources, and @HttpGet, @HttpPost, @HttpPut, @HttpPatch, and @HttpDelete register handlers. Use @HttpMethod("METHOD", options) for other methods. A path on a route is relative to its resource:

Route parameters use :name for one required segment, :name? for an optional final segment, and :name* for zero or more trailing segments (captured as a decoded string joined with /). Static routes take precedence. HEAD uses an explicit handler or falls back to GET with its response body suppressed. An unhandled OPTIONS request is answered with 204 and Allow; a known path with an unsupported method returns 405, and an unknown path returns 404.

Handlers may return values directly (strings are sent as text, other values as JSON) or return new HttpResult(status, body, headers) to specify status, headers, or an empty body.

Parse and validate bodies

Section titled “Parse and validate bodies”

await context.req.parseBody() parses a request body once and reuses the resulting promise. The default body limit is 1 MiB; pass a byte limit or { maxBytes } to change it. Supported content types are JSON and +json, URL-encoded forms, multipart forms, and application/octet-stream (a Buffer). Form fields are strings; repeated names become arrays. Multipart files have { filename, contentType, data }, with data as a Buffer.

Missing or unsupported content types return 415, malformed or interrupted bodies return 400, and bodies over the configured limit return 413. If a route declares a body model, the server validates it before invoking the handler:

Invalid model data returns 422 with field-path issues. A response model validates and shapes JSON output, stripping undeclared fields; use response: { arrayOf: UserResponse } for a list. Response models do not apply to streams or raw responses.

Combine path, query, header, and body values

Section titled “Combine path, query, header, and body values”

For one validated request object, declare each source in @Field metadata. Query, path, and header values arrive as strings and are converted for numeric and boolean field types; ArrayOf supports repeated query parameters. A body is a nested model:

The router validates declared request models before the handler; calling context.req.model() returns the cached model. Invalid path/query/header or body fields return 422, while body parsing retains its 400, 413, and 415 errors. OpenAPI parameters and request-body schema are derived from this metadata. The older server-only @PathParam, @QueryParam, @HeaderParam, and @Body decorators are also available for compatibility.

Cookies

Section titled “Cookies”

context.cookies.get(name) reads a percent-decoded request cookie; getAll(name) returns repeated values. set() appends a Set-Cookie header and clear() expires a cookie:

Options include maxAge in seconds, expires, domain, path, httpOnly, secure, and sameSite. When clearing, pass the same path and domain used to set the cookie. SameSite=None, __Secure-, and __Host- enforce required secure/scope settings. Duplicate names are ambiguous with get(); use getAll(). Malformed cookie headers return 400 when read. Cookie transport is provided, but session storage, token signing, and authentication policy are the application’s responsibility.

Stream responses and large uploads

Section titled “Stream responses and large uploads”

Return an async generator to stream strings or Uint8Array chunks with backpressure, rather than buffering the entire response. Set a content type explicitly; streams otherwise use application/octet-stream:

For uploads, context.req.streamBody({ maxBytes }) returns a one-shot Node readable stream, defaulting to the same 1 MiB limit. Pipe it directly to storage using node:stream/promises pipeline() to preserve backpressure, and pass context.signal to cancel work when the client disconnects. The body can be consumed only once, either buffered with parseBody() or streamed. Limits are checked against both Content-Length and received bytes. Treat client filenames and content types as untrusted; choose storage paths on the server. Multipart parsing is buffered and is intended for smaller uploads.

Build Node.js HTTP APIs from resources, handlers, and validated models.

The @restfx/server package owns Node.js HTTP behavior. Decorated resources organize routes, while models from @restfx/core describe and validate inputs.

Resources and handlers

Section titled “Resources and handlers”

Use @HttpResource(path?) to define a resource and HTTP method decorators to register handlers. Resource-valued fields create nested routes:

This registers GET /api/posts and GET /api/posts/:id. Handlers can return values directly, or use HttpResult to set a status, headers, and response body.

Decorated resource-valued fields are discovered and mounted automatically; use @HttpResource(path?) on a field to override the child path. Children can be provided as instances or constructors, and static or instance fields are supported. For each matched request, RestFX creates a fresh instance of the matched (leaf) resource with its no-argument constructor; state on a supplied leaf instance is not copied. Ancestor resources are shared. Prefer injected services for shared state and request-scoped state rather than storing request data on an ancestor resource.

Request validation

Section titled “Request validation”

Declare a body model in the route options. The server parses and validates the body before invoking the handler:

The server also supports request models assembled from path, query, header, and body values. See request handling for parsing formats, limits, combined request models, cookies, and streaming.

Middleware, services, and OpenAPI

Section titled “Middleware, services, and OpenAPI”

Resources can use scoped middleware, and an IocContainer can provide singleton or request-lifetime services. The server can generate OpenAPI from routes and model metadata, with optional interactive documentation UIs. Follow the guides for dependency injection, middleware and CORS, OpenAPI, and operations.

For all server options and behavior, see the @restfx/server README.
